{{< include _head.qmd >}}

The whole first movement (Adagio sostenuto). Triplets run under a slow melody throughout. The harmony changes slowly, usually once or
twice a bar, so this is a good piece for following an analysis by ear. How to read the labels and use the score:
[Analysed Scores](index.qmd#reading-the-labels).

Things to find:

- the **Neapolitan** (N6) in bar 3 and again later;
- the move to **E major** (the relative major) in bars 7–9;
- the long stretch of dominant harmony (V7 and i64 taking turns, bars 28–41) before the return;
- the **sections** the analysis marks: exposition, development, recapitulation, coda.

Above the score, the **key strip** shows every key the analysts name, in order: c♯, E, e, b, f♯ and home. Click a key to light its bars
and hear them.

{{< include _beethoven-moonlight-1.qmd >}}

## The form, part by part

The outline below summarises a published guide to the movement (a page headed "The Opus 27 Set", p. 161). Press ▶ on a row to light
those bars in the score above and hear them. "Upbeat to" means the part starts on the last beat of the bar before. The outline skips the
first theme's return at bar 42, where the recapitulation begins.

::: {.as-form}
| Bars | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Exposition** | |
| 1–4 | Introduction: the right hand's triplet figure is set going. |
| Upbeat to 5–14 | The first theme, heard twice: first from c♯ minor to E major, then from e minor to b minor. |
| Upbeat to 16–23 | The second theme, also twice, each time starting on a B major chord that sounds like a dominant of e minor that never resolves. The second statement is stretched to end the exposition with a cadence in f♯ minor. |
| **Development** | |
| Upbeat to 24–27 | The opening theme, now starting in f♯ minor, extended. |
| 28–31 | A three-note fragment, perhaps taken from the shape of the second theme. |
| 32–42 | Broken chords unfold: diminished seventh and tonic. |
| 37–42 | Retransition: a melodic fragment in the rhythm of the second theme. Some details here are disputed (the stemming in bar 37, and the uneven phrase lengths in bars 37–39). |
| **Recapitulation** | |
| Upbeat to 52–60 | The second theme, now starting on C♯ major. It sounds like an unresolved dominant of f♯ minor, but the section ends in the home key. |
| Upbeat to 61–69 | Coda: the first theme in the left hand, and a quiet close. |
:::

## The modulations, one by one

The movement uses most of the kinds of modulation in [Chapter 22](../modulation.qmd). Click the bars to hear each one in the score. The
[Modulation](../modulation.qmd) page explains each kind with short examples. The readings are Chen and Su's; where another analyst in
When in Rome, Dmitri Tymoczko, hears it differently, the row says so.

| Bars | From → to | How | Kind ([Ch. 22](../modulation.qmd)) |
|---|---|---|---|
| [▶ 5–9](#){.as-bars data-bars="5-9" data-piece="beethoven-moonlight-1"} | c♯ → E | In bar 7 the F♯ minor chord, iv in c♯, is labelled ii in E: pre-dominant in the new key. E is confirmed by I⁶₄–V⁷–I (bars 8–9). | [Diatonic pivot chord](../modulation.qmd#diatonic-pivot) |
| [▶ 9–10](#){.as-bars data-bars="9-10" data-piece="beethoven-moonlight-1"} | E → e | Same tonic, and the G♯ becomes G♮. There is no pivot: the music simply turns minor. | [Direct](../modulation.qmd#direct) (a change of mode) |
| [▶ 11–14](#){.as-bars data-bars="11-14" data-piece="beethoven-moonlight-1"} | e → b | Bar 11 is V⁴₃/VI in e. The analysis turns to b in bar 12 on a G major chord, VI in b (it is also III in e), and b is confirmed by vii°⁷–V⁶₅–i and i⁶₄–V. Tymoczko hears V⁷/V in e become V⁷ in b instead. | [Diatonic pivot chord](../modulation.qmd#diatonic-pivot); for Tymoczko, a [secondary common chord](../modulation.qmd#chromatic-pivot) |
| [▶ 15–19](#){.as-bars data-bars="15-19" data-piece="beethoven-moonlight-1"} | B major: b or e? | The B major chord of the second theme, taking turns with N6: V/iv in b, a tonicization of e. Nothing cadences in e, which is why the guide calls it a dominant that never resolves. Tymoczko calls it V in e, a modulation. | [Tonicization or modulation?](../modulation.qmd#tonicization) |
| [▶ 19–23](#){.as-bars data-bars="19-23" data-piece="beethoven-moonlight-1"} | → f♯ | f♯ is reached through its own vii°⁶₅ and V⁶₅ and confirmed by i⁶₄–V–i: an authentic cadence ends the exposition. | [Direct](../modulation.qmd#direct) (by the new key's dominant) |
| [▶ 23–27](#){.as-bars data-bars="23-27" data-piece="beethoven-moonlight-1"} | f♯ → c♯ | After V⁶₅ in f♯ (bar 24), the analysis is back in c♯ at bar 25. Tymoczko reads the f♯ minor chord in bar 25 as i in f♯ and iv in c♯, a pivot. | [Direct](../modulation.qmd#direct); for Tymoczko, a [diatonic pivot](../modulation.qmd#diatonic-pivot) |
| [▶ 42–51](#){.as-bars data-bars="42-51" data-piece="beethoven-moonlight-1"} | c♯ → E → c♯ | The recapitulation passes through E only briefly (bars 44–46) before the music returns home. | Compare with bars 5–9 |
| [▶ 52–60](#){.as-bars data-bars="52-60" data-piece="beethoven-moonlight-1"} | C♯ major: f♯ or c♯? | The second theme returns a fourth higher, on C♯ major: V/iv, still in c♯. Tymoczko: V in f♯, back and forth. | [Tonicization or modulation?](../modulation.qmd#tonicization) |
